title: Studying the Southern Surge: How Alabama Beat the Odds in Reading eading
author: Liana Loewus
summary: Commissioned by the Fordham Institute, journalist Liana Loewus visited six elementary schools and interviewed more than 30 state and local leaders, coaches and teachers to explain why Alabama has posted some of the nation's largest early reading gains. Its fourth-grade NAEP reading score is now near the national average for the first time since 2011, and third graders have moved from about 0.6 grade levels below the national average in 2019 to slightly above it in 2025. The report stresses it is not a causal estimate of any one reform. It credits state leadership that understands the science of reading, a multifaceted implementation strategy with approved curricula, a third-grade reading guarantee and a layered coaching pyramid, and steady funding for the Alabama Reading Initiative. It closes by asking whether the gains will survive leadership turnover.
points: Alabama went from the educational basement to near the national average in fourth-grade reading, and was one of only two states to improve NAEP scores between 2019 and 2024.
Mississippi borrowed Alabama's early coaching model, and Alabama has now reinvested in its own second wave of reforms.
Evidence-based reading instruction starts with a state agency that understands the science and pushes districts toward it.
A multifaceted strategy of approved curricula, dedicated coaches, a third-grade reading guarantee and political staying power matters more than any single mandate.
Effective coaching needs defined roles, ample support and steady funding, and sustainability depends on surviving imminent leadership turnover.
quotes: Simply put, there are right and wrong ways to teach reading. And they look pretty similar in Huntsville and Mobile—and Boise and Scranton and Cincinnati.

Skilled reading coaches don’t appear overnight. And they won’t appear at all—and might disappear—if they aren’t properly trained and supported, if the requisite funding doesn’t materialize, or if competing priorities distract them from their primary mission.
No, it’s not cheap, financially or politically. But then again, neither is a systemic failure to teach students to read.

Despite having long been regarded as “America’s educational basement” (to borrow a term from journalist Nicholas Kristof), it has been one of the few states to show academic improvement over the last two rounds of NAEP.
In 2019, Alabama third graders were reading about 0.6 grade levels below the national average; as of 2025, they read at 0.06 grade levels above the national average.
